content.topic: Use of multidetector CTPA for diagnosis of pulmonary embolism (PE) and consideration of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH).
key_points: In patients with low or intermediate clinical probability of PE, a negative CTPA had a high negative predictive value for PE (reported ~96% and ~89%, respectively).
If pre-test probability was high, the negative predictive value of CTPA was lower (~60%).
Positive predictive value of a positive CTPA was high (~92–96%) in patients with intermediate or high clinical probability, but much lower (~58%) in patients with low pre-test likelihood.
Clinicians should consider further testing when clinical judgement and CTPA results are discordant.

Several studies support CTPA as a stand-alone imaging test to exclude PE in patients with low or intermediate clinical probability, but it is controversial whether patients with a negative CTPA and high clinical probability need further investigation.

CTEPH is a potentially fatal late sequela of PE and pre-existing CTEPH should not be missed in patients investigated for suspected acute PE; signs of pre-existing CTEPH are listed in Supplementary Data Table 2 and the diagnosis/management is discussed elsewhere (section 10).
Major strengths, weaknesses/limitations, and radiation issues related to CTPA are summarized in Table 6.

strengths: Readily available around the clock in most centres
Strong validation in prospective management outcome studies
weaknesses_limitations: Limited use in iodine allergy and hyperthyroidism
Risks in pregnant and breastfeeding women
Contraindicated or problematic in severe renal failure
Tendency to overuse because of easy accessibility
radiation_issues: Significant radiation exposure to young female breast tissue
